query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: We hypothesize that laser-based microtexturing of the CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy surface, with tens-of-micrometer-scale dimples or channels, will promote a self-adaptive oxide tribofilm and debris entrapment zone that consistently reduces friction and wear from room temperature to 800 °C when compared to untextured CoCrFeNi.
generation.material_initial_state: Solution-annealed or as-cast CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (polished surface)
generation.intervention: Laser-based microtexturing to form periodic arrays (tens of micrometers in spacing, several micrometers in depth) on the alloy’s sliding surface
generation.conditions: Pin-on-disk or similar unlubricated sliding tests from 25 °C up to 800 °C in ambient air under normal loads of 2–10 N
generation.structural_mediator: Microtextured dimples that trap wear debris and promote stable oxide tribofilm formation at elevated temperatures
generation.mechanism: Controlled surface patterning enhances oxide film retention and reduces abrasive contact by directing debris into the microtextured recesses, enabling consistent low-friction sliding and minimal wear over a broad temperature range
generation.predicted_outcome: A stable friction coefficient at or below that of the untextured alloy throughout 25–800 °C, along with a reduced wear rate of at least 20% relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi sample
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi alloy tested under identical tribological conditions (no laser texturing)
generation.boundary: Effective in air at temperatures up to 800 °C and loads up to 10 N; applicability in corrosive or vacuum environments remains unverified
generation.uncertainty: Stability of the oxide film at the highest temperatures and under varying humidity or oxidation conditions is not fully established; microstructure changes at high temperature could degrade tribofilm formation or adhesion

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare CoCrFeNi coupons, half of which are laser-microtextured under identical parameter settings. Conduct identical pin-on-disk tests at increments from 25 °C to 800 °C in air, measuring friction coefficient and wear volume under 2–10 N loads.
measurements: Steady-state coefficient of friction values compared between microtextured and untextured samples at each temperature
Wear track cross-sectional profiles to determine material loss
Surface and subsurface characterization (SEM/EDS) of tribo-oxide layers and debris accumulation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If microtexturing does not yield consistently lower friction and wear across the temperature range (i.e., if the microtextured samples do not show at least a 20% reduction in wear rate and a consistently lower coefficient of friction compared to the untextured baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

decision.trend: Starting in 2017, researchers explored oxide dispersion (PMC5706259) to enhance the abrasive wear resistance of CrMnFeCoNi-type HEAs at room temperature but did not fully address high-temperature sliding. By 2020, work on CoCrFeMnNi in inert environments (PMC7311485) demonstrated low friction via a near-surface nanocrystalline layer formed under contact stresses, yet it left open questions about performance in broader temperature and environmental regimes. Subsequent studies (e.g., PMC9960858) showed that grain refinement improves wear resistance, but without detailing how to maintain consistently low friction up to 800 °C under varying loads. Recent advances in designing hierarchical microstructures in other complex concentrated alloys (PMC10241162) revealed excellent sliding performance between room temperature and 800 °C, but such architectures have not yet been demonstrated specifically for the CoCrFeNi system—that remains the key gap.
decision.unsolved: Although CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloys excel in both strength and ductility, their ability to sustain low friction and wear under diverse operating conditions (temperature excursions to 800 °C, variable loads, and reactive environments) remains poorly understood. A unifying strategy that maintains a protective surface layer, particularly above 600 °C, and addresses the fundamental tribological response of CoCrFeNi over a wide range of temperatures is still elusive.
decision.lever: Laser-based microtexturing to create a self-adaptive oxide tribofilm at the surface, with controlled spacing (tens of micrometers) and depth (micrometers) patterning to promote stable oxide glazing and debris entrapment
decision.why: Prior studies show that nanocrystalline layers or in situ-formed oxide films can significantly reduce friction and wear in high-entropy alloys, but they often do not remain stable under fluctuating temperatures up to 800 °C. By combining laser texturing (which can trap wear debris and support oxide film formation) with the inherent oxidation tendencies of CoCrFeNi, the surface can adapt in sliding contact and continuously regenerate protective oxides. This design leverages known benefits of tribo-oxide layering from references like PMC7311485 and PMC10241162 and applies them specifically to CoCrFeNi in a way that both fosters beneficial debris retention (thus minimizing abrasive wear) and promotes a robust, thermally stable lubricious film, maintaining friction and wear at or below the levels of the untextured alloy at lower temperatures. The hypothesis would be invalidated if high-temperature sliding tests (e.g., using a pin-on-disk setup at temperatures incrementally from room temperature to 800 °C under typical load conditions of 2–10 N in air) show that textured surfaces fail to form or retain an oxide tribofilm and exhibit significantly higher coefficients of friction or wear rates relative to the unmodified CoCrFeNi material.
